title: Believing sinners differ from unbelievers: they can do good works from faith
source_text: XLVII. Istud videre est apud Jansenium De statu naturae lapsae libro quarto capite quarto. Nam, inquit, quamvis verissimum sit opera peccatorum omnium, imo etiam justorum, quae non referuntur ad eum finem ad quem referri debent, hoc est, ad Deum, sed in creaturis haerent, vera esse peccata: falsum est tamen eandem de peccatoribus fidelibus, quam infidelibus esse rationem. Hoc ipso enim quo peccatores fide imbuti sunt, quanquam perfecta illa charitate Deum super omnia diligente, hoc est, justificatione, destituti sint, multa tamen bona ex illa fide operari possunt; sicut in primis ipsum credere & operari velle, & si adhuc viribus careant, infirmitatem suam ingemiscere, ex fide justificationem, vel operandi vires impetrare, cujusmodi opera Augustinus semper peccatoribus tribuit. Et postea probare volens fideles quantislibet peccatis mancipatos non carere imperfecto quodam amore Dei, qui sincerus tamen sit & verae pietatis initium, quali Dei amore carent prorsus infideles, Hoc ipso, inquit, quo adhuc fideles permanent, non possunt non habere affectum illum verae pietatis atque dilectionis, ex quo credunt Deo, ex quo sperant subinde beatitudinem, ex quo orant pro impetranda perfecta charitate, atque justitia; ex quo etiam alia nonnulla bona sincero Dei intuitu operantur, quamvis necdum ita diligant, ut eum omnibus terrenis amoribus, ac delectationibus praeferant.
pass_a_gloss: XLVII. That is seen in Jansenius On the state of fallen nature book four chapter four. For, he says, although it is most true that the works of all sinners, nay even of the just, which are not referred to that end to which they ought to be referred, that is, to God, but stick in creatures, are true sins: it is false yet that the reason is the same of faithful sinners, as of unbelievers. For by this very thing that sinners are imbued with faith, although destitute of that perfect charity loving God above all, that is, of justification, yet many good things they can work from that faith; as first of all believing itself and willing to work, and if they still lack strength, to groan over their infirmity, from faith to obtain justification, or strength to work, which kind of works Augustine always attributes to sinners. And afterward wishing to prove that the faithful enslaved to however many sins lack not a certain imperfect love of God, which yet is sincere and the beginning of true piety, which love of God unbelievers altogether lack, By this very thing, he says, that they still remain faithful, they cannot not have that affection of true piety and love, from which they believe God, from which they hope for beatitude in due course, from which they pray for obtaining perfect charity, and justice; from which also they work some other good things with sincere regard to God, although they do not yet so love, as to prefer him to all earthly loves, and delights.
pass_b_english: This is seen in Jansenius, On the state of fallen nature, book 4, chapter 4. 'Although it is most true,' he says, 'that the works of all sinners, and even of the righteous, which are not referred to the end to which they ought to be referred, that is, to God, but stick fast in creatures, are true sins, it is false that the case is the same for believing sinners as for unbelievers.

For by the very fact that sinners are imbued with faith, even though they lack that perfect charity which loves God above all, that is, justification, they can still do many good things from that faith: first of all, believing itself and willing to act, and, if they still lack the strength, groaning over their weakness and obtaining from faith justification or the strength to act. Augustine always ascribes works of this kind to sinners.'

Later, wishing to prove that believers, however enslaved to sins, do not lack a certain imperfect love of God, which is nonetheless sincere and the beginning of true piety, a love of God that unbelievers wholly lack, he says: 'By the very fact that they still remain believers they cannot fail to have that affection of true piety and love from which they believe God, from which they hope for blessedness in due course, from which they pray to obtain perfect charity and righteousness, and from which they also do some other good things with a sincere regard to God, although they do not yet love him so as to prefer him to all earthly loves and delights.'

choices.why: The theological virtue by which God is loved for his own sake; Jansenius sets it against cupiditas as the only two loves, so the technical 'charity' is kept rather than 'love'.
